Many AI experts worry about powerful AI getting into the hands of bad actors—those who might use such powerful AI to cause damage or for personal gain that inflicts costs on others—via hacking. A bad actor might be a black hat hacker, a terrorist group, or a rogue state.

One way to decrease the chance of this type of hacking succeeding is for those building powerful AI, the leading AI labs, to have strong cybersecurity measures in place. Given how high the stakes might be (see, e.g., “[AI risk](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/topics/ai-risk)”), policymakers may decide to not bank on AI labs attaining strong enough cybersecurity by default.

question_details.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if, by Dec 31, 2025, there is a federal law which requires all U.S. actors in possession of AI models fitting certain criteria to take measures to secure those models. The law must be designed to promote security of _powerful_ models, rather than, for example, models that might compromise individuals' privacy if stolen. If necessary, this will be decided by a judging panel made up of the Metaculus AI Forecasting team, or, failing that (e.g., because the AI Forecasting team no longer exists), at least 3 Metaculus admins: the judging panel would consider the stated intent of those who proposed the initial version of the bill.
question_details.fine_print: There may well be overlap between the most powerful models and the models that most compromise privacy. For this question’s resolution, what matters is whether the law is _intended_ to secure _powerful_ models.

This move responds to the rapid growth of AI in China, which ranks second globally in the World Artificial Intelligence Innovation Index and saw its generative AI user base reach 515 million by June 2025—double the number from December 2024. According to the National Computer Virus Emergency Response Center, AI-related cyber threats rose significantly in 2025, with network attacks accounting for 29% and data breaches for 26% of incidents. The amendment aligns the Cybersecurity Law with other key legislation, including the Civil Code and the Personal Information Protection Law, to improve legal coordination and enforcement. Penalties for violations have been strengthened, with potential sanctions including suspension, closure, or revocation of business licenses. In March 2025, the CAC and relevant departments further developed a second draft for public comment. The first review of the draft amendment occurred at the 17th session of the 14th Standing Committee in September 2025. On October 23, 2025, Wang Xiang, spokesperson for the Legislative Affairs Commission of the NPC Standing Committee, reported that during the public consultation period from September 12 to October 11, 108 individuals submitted 162 comments. Based on feedback, the draft was revised to: (1) strengthen the guiding principles of cybersecurity work; (2) add provisions promoting AI safety and development; (3) improve alignment with the Civil Code and the Personal Information Protection Law in personal data protection; and (4) refine penalty provisions.
